title: Fifth commandment: health (CCC 2288–2301)
hook: care for health, and respect for the dead

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth commandment in Cain's field: every life is sacred, and peace starts with anger. Your line was every life.

Goal reached, ten thousand steps, says the wristband. Down the street, another man hasn't seen a doctor in six years and jokes that his body will let him know. And in an old story from the Bible, a man named Tobit leaves his dinner untasted, goes out, and carries home the body of a murdered man lying in the street, so he can bury him after sunset. Three ways of treating a body, living and dead.
screen: `A WRISTBAND BUZZES.` → `SIX YEARS WITHOUT A DOCTOR.` → `TOBIT LEAVES HIS DINNER.`

segments.voice: The Catechism calls life and physical health precious gifts entrusted to us by God. So we take reasonable care of them, keeping in mind the needs of others and the common good. Society, it adds, should help people find food, clothing, housing, health care, schooling and work. Health is never only private. Then a sharp turn. Morality respects bodily life but doesn't make it an absolute. The Catechism rejects what it calls a cult of the body: sacrificing everything for it, idolizing physical perfection and success at sports. The body is a gift to care for, not a god to serve. In between sits temperance: avoiding every kind of excess, the abuse of food, alcohol, tobacco or medicine. Those who put others in danger by drunkenness or reckless speed, it says plainly, are gravely guilty, and using drugs, except on strictly medical grounds, is a grave offense. Then it follows the body to the end. The dying should be given attention and care, to live their last moments in dignity and peace, surrounded by prayer. The bodies of the dead must be treated with respect and charity, in faith and hope of the resurrection; burying the dead is a work of mercy. That's Tobit, whose journey you followed in year two, leaving his dinner to carry a dead man home. Organ donation after death can be a noble act, and cremation is permitted, as long as it isn't chosen as a denial of faith in the resurrection. From the gym to the graveside: care for the body, honor it, but don't worship it.
screen: `HEALTH: A GIFT ENTRUSTED.` · `NOT A CULT OF THE BODY.` · `TEMPERANCE: NO EXCESS.` · `THE DEAD, TREATED WITH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Starting at your feet, move your attention slowly upward and notice each part without judging it: tension, tiredness, hunger, pain. Choose one small, reasonable kindness for your body today: a glass of water, a walk, an early night, the appointment you keep putting off. If you pray, thank God for this body as a gift; if not, thank it plainly for carrying you this far.
Fifth commandment. Respect for life includes reasonable care for health, temperance, and respect for the dying and the dead, without making the body an idol. Today's word.
Your line: care, not worship. Living or dead, the body is owed respect. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Catholics are taught to care for their health with temperance, to accompany the dying with prayer and the sacraments, and to bury the dead with a funeral Mass, a corporal work of mercy.

chat.says: Does Catholic teaching care about health, or only about souls?
options: It does: health is a gift to care for with temperance, but the Catechism warns against a cult of the body.
Health is the highest good, so the Catechism says to sacrifice anything to keep the body fit.
It cares only after death: funerals are covered, but daily health isn't mentioned at all.
chat.meaning: The Catechism calls health a precious gift to care for reasonably, asks for temperance, and rejects idolizing the body.
